draft.title: Australia as a social laboratory
card: Around 1900, Australia was called a social laboratory. Its colonies and then the new nation tried reforms that few other places had tried.
Secret ballot
voters mark their choice in private. Victoria and South Australia brought it in during the 1850s, and it later spread to many other countries.
Votes for women
South Australia gave women the vote in 1894. Federal law gave most non-Indigenous women the vote in 1902.
Harvester case

in 1907 a judge set a basic wage meant to let a worker support a family. The age pension, which paid older people an income, became national in 1909. Many Aboriginal people were left out of these reforms, and the 1902 law mostly kept them from voting.
draft.remember: Early Australia led the way on reforms such as the secret ballot, votes for women, a basic wage and the pension, but many Aboriginal people were left out.

a.q: Why was early Australia called a social laboratory?
opts: It tried new reforms that few other places had tried
It tested new medicines on its colonial population
It copied every political reform made in Britain
It banned all change to the way people voted
a.why: The name refers to reforms such as the secret ballot and votes for women, which were tried early in Australia. It was not about science or copying Britain. The reforms were new ideas, not a ban on change.
a.clue: Think of a laboratory as a place where new things are tried out.

b.q: In 1908 a newspaper in Melbourne praises Australia's reforms as fair to all its people. Which fact from the card best shows that this claim was too broad?
opts: The 1902 law mostly kept Aboriginal people from voting
South Australia gave women the vote in 1894
A basic wage was set in the Harvester case of 1907
The secret ballot began in the 1850s
b.why: The 1902 voting law left out many Aboriginal people, so the reforms did not reach everyone. The other three options are real reforms, and they support the idea that Australia led the way rather than showing who was left out.
b.clue: Look for the fact about who was left out, not who gained.

a.best: It tried new reforms that few other places had tried

b.best: The 1902 law mostly kept Aboriginal people from voting

proposal.title: Australia as a social laboratory
card: Social laboratory
a name given to Australia around 1900. Its colonies and then the new nation tested reforms in voting, work and welfare that few other countries had tried.
Voting

the secret ballot, where voters mark their choice in private, began in Victoria and South Australia in the 1850s, and other countries later copied it. South Australia gave women the vote in 1894, and federal law gave most non-Indigenous women the vote in 1902.
Work and welfare
in the Harvester case of 1907, a judge set a basic wage meant to let a worker support a family. The age pension, an income paid to older people, became national in 1909.
Who was left out
the 1902 voting law mostly kept Aboriginal people from voting in federal elections. The age pension law left most of them out as well.
proposal.remember: Australia tested new reforms early, but Aboriginal people were mostly left out of them.

a.q: Why is the secret ballot of the 1850s an example of Australia as a social laboratory?
opts: Few places had tried it, and other nations later copied it
It let every adult in the colonies vote for the first time
It came from Britain, where voters had used it for years
It made voting compulsory for all men in the colonies
a.why: Victoria and South Australia tried the secret ballot before most places, and other countries later took it up. That is what being a social laboratory means. It did not give every adult the vote: South Australian women waited until 1894.
a.clue: Think about where the idea started and where it went next.

b.q: In 1908 a newspaper in Melbourne praises Australia's reforms as fair to all its people. Which fact from the card best shows that this claim was too broad?
opts: The 1902 law mostly kept Aboriginal people from voting
South Australia gave women the vote in 1894
A basic wage was set in the Harvester case of 1907
The secret ballot began in the 1850s
b.why: The 1902 voting law left out most Aboriginal people, so the reforms did not reach everyone. The other three options are real reforms, and they support the idea that Australia tried new ideas rather than showing who was left out.
b.clue: Look for the fact about who was left out, not who gained.
